newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan heads for uncertainty as Bhutto fights on.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan heads for uncertainty as Bhutto fights on.

text.p: Pakistan headed into new uncertainty on Thursday after a defiant Benazir Bhutto demanded that the president resign and vowed to recapture power.

Late on Wednesday the ousted pime minister was given permission to visit her detained husband Asif Ali Zardari after she had threatened to bring kidnapping charges against President Farooq Leghari, who sacked her three-year government on Tuesday.

Shah Mahmood Qureshi, a spokesman for Bhutto, said he had gone with her and former interior minister Naseerullah Babar to Sihala resthouse near Islamabad on Wednesday night, but after a four-hour wait Zardari had still not been produced.
"We went to Sihala resthouse at 9.30 p.m. and were told that Zardari would be brought there, but by 1.30 a.m. he still had not shown up, and then I left," Qureshi said.

Qureshi, former parliamentary affairs minister, said Bhutto and Babar had remained behind at the official resthouse, and it remained unclear whether Bhutto had seen her husband. "I have had no telephone contact with them since then," he said.

Zardari was picked up by soldiers in Lahore on Tuesday and later transferred to Rawalpindi. The caretaker government said on Wednesday that he was in "protective custody," but did not clarify the grounds on which he was being held.
A combative Bhutto, speaking on Wednesday at her first news conference since being dislodged, demanded the resignation of Leghari and promised to fight her dismissal in court.
"I'm an elected prime minister and I'll be prime minister again," she said.

Leghari had justified his dismissal of Bhutto's government on the grounds that it was paralysed by corruption, nepotism and misrule, and had allowed security forces to kill "thousands of people" in the southern city of Karachi and elsewhere.

"We expect the court to restore the (National) Assembly within a month," Bhutto told the packed news conference in the prime minister's residence, where police had kept her in custody for 36 hours before lifting curbs on her movements.
Bhutto accused Leghari of ordering the kidnapping of her husband, a businessman and former investment minister.

"I believe that my husband Asif Ali Zardari...has been kidnapped on your orders since yesterday morning," she said in a hand-written letter to Leghari, copies of which were distributed at her news conference.
Zardari is the target of corruption allegations levelled against Bhutto's government. He has denied any wrongdoing.
"Asif Zardari is in protective custody. It means there is something against him, some inquiry may be on, or something else may be considered," Information Minister Irshad Haqqani said.
Bhutto's pledge to fight to the finish added fresh uncertainty to an already turbulent political scene.

Calling on voters to elect "honest, able and God-fearing people", Leghari on Tuesday set general elections for next February. But the timetable could be upset by Bhutto's legal challenge, which seemed sure to prolong the political crisis.
Bhutto noted that the Supreme Court had reinstated the government of her main political opponent Nawaz Sharif after it had been dismissed by then-president Ghulam Ishaq Khan in 1993.
"I will go to the court expecting justice," she said.
The caretaker government, meeting under Prime Minister Meraj Khalid for the first time on Wednesday, appealed to citizens to send evidence of corruption to the Interior Minister.
The cabinet also cut ministers' salaries in half and barred them from travelling first class as part of an austerity package aimed at trimming spending and checking the "VIP culture".
